sections.heading: From implementation to direction
sections.content: Wu contrasts the enjoyable work of thinking through architecture and what to build—which he estimates takes about 10% of an average engineer’s time—with implementation and maintenance work, which he says takes about 90%. He describes Devin’s aim as moving engineers “from bricklayer to architect”: engineers specify what they want and direct the work, while retaining control and multiplying what they can build. [S1]

sections.heading: What engineers do in practice
sections.content: Engineers can hand off tasks asynchronously, sometimes working with up to five Devins at once. Their role is to define precisely what is being built and where their expertise is needed, then steer complex changes—for example, setting how a class should be structured and asking for downstream references to be updated. Devin does the bulk of the work. [S3]

sections.heading: More emphasis on architectural judgment
sections.content: Wu says routine implementation and boilerplate have become faster with AI. He sees greater value in understanding complex systems and company context, identifying which problems to solve, choosing solutions, and weighing key decisions and trade-offs. At his company, he says engineers also spend more time thinking about how to improve Devin, its interface, and its workflow. [S2, S4]

sections.content: Wu contrasts architecture and planning—the part of engineering he finds most enjoyable—with routine implementation and maintenance, which he says can take about 90% of an average engineer’s time, leaving roughly 10% for that higher-level thinking. Devin is intended to move engineers from “bricklayer to architect”: the human remains in control and specifies what to build, while gaining the ability to build more in a given amount of time.

sections.heading: How the work changes
sections.content: Engineers can hand off tasks asynchronously, sometimes running up to five Devins at once. They focus their attention on defining precisely what is being solved and built, steering more complex changes, and reviewing or testing where needed; Devin does the bulk of the work. Wu describes the shift as using an interface to hand off and build tasks, not as conventional people management.

sections.heading: Skills that become more important
sections.content: Wu says engineers should lean into understanding complex systems and the wider company and product context: identifying which problems to solve, how to solve them, the solution to build, and the important decisions and trade-offs. He also emphasizes thinking precisely, understanding abstractions, and being able to “peel back” their layers. At his company, engineers also spend more time asking how to improve Devin and what interface, workflow, or features will make it a better experience.

sections.content: Wu says engineers often spend much of their time on implementation and operational work, while the enjoyable core of engineering is defining the problem, thinking through the architecture and details, and mapping out what the computer should do. Devin is intended to move engineers from “bricklayer to architect”: they specify what they want and direct the work, with the human still in control and responsible for the full specification. sections.content: Engineers can hand tasks to multiple Devins asynchronously—Wu said many on his team work with up to five at once—and focus their own effort where expertise matters: defining the solution, handling complex parts, and steering changes. For example, an engineer might specify how a class should be structured and that downstream references should change too. Devin does the bulk of the work; the engineer gives feedback or checks the result as needed. [S3, S12]
